claim: Humans do not point their ears as they focus attention on novel, salient, or task-relevant stimuli.
source: Unlike dogs and cats, people do not point their ears as they focus attention on novel, salient, or task-relevant stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about human anatomy and behavior compared to other mammals.

claim: Humans may have retained a vestigial pinna-orienting system that has persisted as a 'neural fossil' within the brain for about 25 million years.
source: Our species may nevertheless have retained a vestigial pinna-orienting system that has persisted as a 'neural fossil' within in the brain for about 25 million years.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the paper, supported by the experimental data presented and evolutionary reasoning discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The direction of auditory attention is reflected in sustained electrical activity of muscles within the vestigial auriculomotor system.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we demonstrate that the direction of auditory attention is reflected in sustained electrical activity of muscles within the vestigial auriculomotor system.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by EMG data from both experiments.

claim: EMG recordings showed larger activity at the ear on the side of the attended stimulus during both reflexive and voluntary attention.
source: In both experiments, EMG recordings showed larger activity at the ear on the side of the attended stimulus, but with slightly different patterns.
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data presented in Figures 2-6.

claim: Upward movement (perking) differed according to the lateral focus of attention only during voluntary orienting.
source: Upward movement (perking) differed according to the lateral focus of attention only during voluntary orienting
evidence: This is supported by the SAM muscle data showing significant effects only in Experiment 2 (voluntary attention).

claim: Rearward folding of the pinna's upper-lateral edge exhibited differences according to attention direction only during reflexive orienting.
source: rearward folding of the pinna's upper-lateral edge exhibited such differences only during reflexive orienting.
evidence: This is supported by the TAM muscle data showing significant effects only in Experiment 1 (reflexive attention).

claim: Higher primates have lost the ability to orient by adjusting pinna shape and focal direction.
source: Ear movements are not a useful cue in humans or apes because higher primates have lost the ability to orient by adjusting pinna shape and focal direction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about primate evolution and anatomy.

claim: Wilson's oculo-auricular phenomenon involves shifting the gaze hard to one side eliciting a 1 to 4 mm deflection of the lateral rim of both ears.
source: The first was Wilson's oculo-auricular phenomenon (Wilson, 1908), in which shifting the gaze hard to one side elicits a 1 to 4 mm deflection of the lateral rim of both ears.
evidence: This is cited from Wilson, 1908 as prior research.

claim: The relevance of Wilson's oculo-auricular phenomenon to spatial attention is uncertain with diverging results across studies.
source: The relevance to spatial attention is uncertain, though, with diverging results across studies, for example see Gerstle and Wilkinson, 1929; Urban et al., 1993; O'Beirne and Patuzzi, 1999.
evidence: This is based on citations to multiple prior studies showing inconsistent results.

claim: The bilateral postauricular muscle (PAM) reflex has an onset latency of 10 ms to acoustic onset transients.
source: Additional evidence comes from a 1987 study (Hackley et al., 1987) of the bilateral postauricular muscle (PAM) reflex (onset latency = 10 ms) to acoustic onset transients.
evidence: This is cited from Hackley et al., 1987.

claim: Increased PAM reflex amplitudes were observed when subjects directed their attention to a stream of tones on the same side as the recorded muscle while ignoring a competing, contralateral stream.
source: Increased amplitudes were observed when subjects directed their attention to a stream of tones on the same side as the recorded muscle while ignoring a competing, contralateral stream.
evidence: This is cited from Hackley et al., 1987.

claim: Comparisons across left/right stimulus, attention, and PAM combinations localized modulation to the motor limb of the reflex arc.
source: Comparisons across left/right stimulus, attention, and PAM combinations localized modulation to the motor limb of the reflex arc.
evidence: This is cited from Hackley et al., 1987.

claim: The automatic capture of attention by unexpected sounds coming from a speaker hidden to the left of the participant elicited greater activity in the left than right PAM.
source: Finally, an experiment in Stekelenburg and van Boxtel, 2002 found that the automatic capture of attention by unexpected sounds coming from a speaker hidden to the left of the participant elicited greater activity in the left than right PAM.
evidence: This is cited from Stekelenburg and van Boxtel, 2002.

claim: The signal-averaged EMG waveforms show well-defined responses with an onset latency of about 70 ms.
source: The signal-averaged EMG waveforms of Figure 2 show well-defined responses with an onset latency of about 70 ms, responses that vary in amplitude, duration, and morphology according to the relative direction of the sound source.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Posterior, ipsilateral stimulation elicited the most vigorous responses from PAM, AAM, and TAM.
source: Posterior, ipsilateral stimulation elicited the most vigorous responses from these three muscles.
evidence: This is supported by the interaction effects in the statistical analysis.

claim: The vestigial auriculomotor drive appears to be causally linked to very small ear displacements.
source: The corresponding vestigial auriculomotor drive appears to be causally linked to very small ear displacements, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Video 1, and Video 2.
evidence: This is supported by video analysis showing submillimeter pinna displacements correlated with EMG activity.

claim: TAM activity reflected lateralization of transient, exogenous attention but not sustained, goal-directed attention.
source: Whereas TAM but not SAM activity had reflected lateralization of transient, exogenous attention, the reverse was true for sustained, goal-directed attention.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the results of Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: EMG energy of all three muscles (PAM, AAM, SAM) is sustained across the 5-min sessions in Experiment 2.
source: Although PAM activity declines over time, EMG energy of all three muscles is clearly sustained across the 5-min sessions, see Figure 6.
evidence: This is shown in the time-resolved analysis in Figure 6.

claim: There is a complete absence of eye movements that were systematically related to attention direction in both experiments.
source: Figure 7 and Figure 8 document a complete absence of eye movements that were systematically related to attention direction.
evidence: This is supported by EOG analysis shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Electro-oculographic recordings have a resolution of only 1-2 degrees.
source: A limitation of these findings is that electro-oculographic recordings have a resolution of only 1 − 2°.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of the EOG measurement technique.

claim: Gaze shifts less than 30 degrees are rarely accompanied by auriculomotor activity.
source: However, gaze shifts less than 30° are rarely accompanied by auriculomotor activity, see Urban et al., 1993.
evidence: This is cited from Urban et al., 1993.

claim: Activation of TAM during Wilson's oculo-auricular phenomenon is more vigorous on the side opposite the direction of gaze.
source: Activation of TAM during Wilson's oculo-auricular phenomenon is more vigorous on the side opposite the direction of gaze, see Gerstle and Wilkinson, 1929; Urban et al., 1993.
evidence: This is cited from Gerstle and Wilkinson, 1929 and Urban et al., 1993.

claim: TAM activation was relatively enhanced at the ear on the same side as the attention-engaging sounds in Experiment 1.
source: By contrast, we found in Experiment one that TAM activation was relatively enhanced at the ear on the same side as the attention-engaging sounds.
evidence: This is supported by the EMG data from Experiment 1.

claim: The PAM component of Wilson's phenomenon exhibits enhanced activity on the ipsilateral side, but this effect appears to be reliable only for gaze shifts greater than about 40 degrees.
source: The PAM component of Wilson's phenomenon does exhibit enhanced activity on the ipsilateral side, but this effect appears to be reliable only for gaze shifts greater than about 40 degrees (Patuzzi and O'Beirne, 1999, Figure 4).
evidence: This is cited from Patuzzi and O'Beirne, 1999.

claim: Recent research has shown that azimuthal head rotations have little effect on auricular activity in humans.
source: However, recent research has shown that azimuthal head rotations have little effect on auricular activity in humans, see Cook and Patuzzi, 2014.
evidence: This is cited from Cook and Patuzzi, 2014.

claim: Analysis of sternocleidomastoid EMG suggests that movements of the neck were rare, small, and unsystematic.
source: Moreover, analysis of sternocleidomastoid EMG in our data suggest that movements of the neck were rare, small, and unsystematic, see Figure 7—figure supplements 4 and 5.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of sternocleidomastoid EMG data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Head rotations would have been too slow to generate the rapid responses of around 70 ms onset latency observed in the ear muscles in Experiment 1.
source: Finally, head rotations would have been too slow to generate the rapid responses of around 70 ms onset latency observed in the ear muscles in Experiment 1.
evidence: This is inferred from the known speed of head movements compared to the observed EMG onset latencies.

claim: There was no corresponding co-activation of the zygomaticus and frontalis muscles.
source: Note that there was also no corresponding co–activation of the other measured (non–auricular) facial muscles, the zygomaticus and frontalis muscle, see Figure 7—figure supplements 6–9 for Experiment one and Figure 8—figure supplement 2 for Experiment 2.
evidence: This is supported by EMG analysis of these control muscles shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The neural drive to human ear muscles is so weak that the actual movements are at least one to two orders of magnitude smaller compared to those generated during biting, smiling, grimacing, or voluntary ear-wiggling.
source: The neural drive to our ear muscles is so weak that the actual movements (see co-registered video data in the Supplementary Information) are at least one to two orders of magnitude smaller compared to those generated during biting, smiling, grimacing, or voluntary ear-wiggling.
evidence: This is inferred from the video analysis and comparison with other facial movements.

claim: The ability to swivel and point the pinnae seems to have been lost during the transition from the primarily nocturnal lifestyles of prosimians to the diurnal ones of New World monkeys, and then, Old World monkeys.
source: The ability to swivel and point the pinnae seems to have been lost during the transition from the primarily nocturnal lifestyles of prosimians to the diurnal ones of New World monkeys, and then, Old World monkeys (Coleman and Ross, 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Coleman and Ross, 2004.

claim: Pinna mobility continued to decline as the ears became shorter and more rigid.
source: Mobility continued to decline as the ears became shorter and more rigid, see Waller et al., 2008; Coleman and Ross, 2004.
evidence: This is cited from Waller et al., 2008 and Coleman and Ross, 2004.

claim: An inferior auricular muscle to oppose SAM still exists in lesser apes such as gibbons and siamangs but not in chimpanzees or humans.
source: For example, an inferior auricular muscle to oppose SAM still exists in lesser apes such as gibbons and siamangs (Burrows et al., 2011), but not in chimpanzees (Burrows et al., 2011) or humans (Cattaneo and Pavesi, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Burrows et al., 2011 and Cattaneo and Pavesi, 2014.

claim: It is likely that the vestibulo-auricular reflex as documented in cats has not been conserved in humans.
source: Given that head rotation has little effect on PAM activity (Cook and Patuzzi, 2014), it seems likely that the vestibulo–auricular reflex as documented in cats (Tollin et al., 2009) has not been conserved in our species.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited evidence about head rotation effects and comparison with cats.

claim: The ability to use proprioceptive information to adjust auditory processing in accordance with pinna position, orientation, and shape as documented in cats is presumably lost in humans.
source: Also presumably lost is the ability to use proprioceptive information to adjust auditory processing in accordance with pinna position, orientation, and shape as documented in cats, see Kanold and Young, 2001.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of muscle spindles in human ear muscles and comparison with cats.

claim: The ear muscles of Old World monkeys have spindles.
source: Although the ear muscles of Old World monkeys have spindles (Lovell et al., 1977), those of humans do not (Cattaneo and Pavesi, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Lovell et al., 1977.

claim: The ear muscles of humans do not have spindles.
source: Although the ear muscles of Old World monkeys have spindles (Lovell et al., 1977), those of humans do not (Cattaneo and Pavesi, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Cattaneo and Pavesi, 2014.

claim: When pinna-orienting movements became too small to modify acoustic input substantially, possibly 25 million years ago when lesser apes branched off from Old World monkeys, selective environmental pressure ceased.
source: When pinna-orienting movements became too small to modify acoustic input substantially, possibly 25 million years ago when lesser apes branched off from Old World monkeys, see Gibbs et al., 2007 as discussed in Hackley, 2015, selective environmental pressure ceased.
evidence: This is cited from Gibbs et al., 2007 and Hackley, 2015, and represents an evolutionary inference.

claim: The neural system for pinna-orienting became more-or-less 'frozen' in a form optimized for controlling taller, more flexible ears, mounted on a smaller, more spherical head.
source: The neural system became more-or-less 'frozen' in a form optimized for controlling taller, more flexible ears, mounted on a smaller, more spherical head.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on the vestigial nature of the system.

claim: Co-activation of opposing muscles AAM and PAM in remote human ancestors would have reduced occlusion of the ear canal by the tragus.
source: Co-activation of opposing muscles AAM and PAM in our remote ancestors would have reduced occlusion of the ear canal by the tragus.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed co-activation pattern and comparison with monkeys.

claim: Occlusion of the ear canal by the tragus occurs in monkeys when contraction of the PAM homolog is unopposed.
source: Note that this occlusion occurs in monkeys when contraction of the PAM homolog is unopposed, see Waller et al., 2008, supplementary video clip 17.
evidence: This is cited from Waller et al., 2008.

claim: PAM-AAM co-activation would have stabilized the base of the pinna and reduced myotendinous elasticity, thereby allowing quick changes in position or orientation.
source: In addition, PAM-AAM co-activation would have stabilized the base of the pinna and reduced myotendinous elasticity, thereby allowing quick changes in position or orientation.
evidence: This is inferred from biomechanical principles.

claim: A study of pinna orienting in cats showed that they tend to tilt the ear downward slightly when orienting to a lateral target.
source: A study of pinna orienting in cats, whose tall ears resemble those of prosimians, showed that they tend to tilt the ear downward slightly when orienting to a lateral target, see Populin and Yin, 1998.
evidence: This is cited from Populin and Yin, 1998.

claim: Neurobiologists have distinguished two types of pinna-orienting movements in cats based on onset latency.
source: Neurobiologists have distinguished two types of pinna-orienting movements in cats, based on onset latency, see Siegmund and Santibáñez, 1982.
evidence: This is cited from Siegmund and Santibáñez, 1982.

claim: The short-latency pinna response in cats is specific to auditory stimuli and is chronometrically uncorrelated with saccades toward the target.
source: The short-latency response is specific to auditory stimuli and is chronometrically uncorrelated with saccades toward the target.
evidence: This is cited from Siegmund and Santibáñez, 1982.

claim: The long-latency pinna response in cats can be elicited by visual as well as auditory stimuli and it is roughly synchronous with ocular orienting.
source: By contrast, the long-latency response can be elicited by visual as well as auditory stimuli and it is roughly synchronous with ocular orienting, see Populin and Yin, 1998.
evidence: This is cited from Populin and Yin, 1998.

claim: Cats' unconditioned pinna responses to sounds from a 4-speaker setup had an EMG onset latency that averaged 78 ms.
source: Using a 4-speaker set-up similar to that of the present Experiment 1, Siegmund and Santibáñez, 1982 found cats' unconditioned pinna responses to have an EMG onset latency that averaged 78 ms, similar to our value of about 70 ms.
evidence: This is cited from Siegmund and Santibáñez, 1982.

claim: When cats were trained to make gaze shifts toward sound sources, onset latency of the auriculomotor responses dropped to a remarkable 29 ms.
source: The animals were then trained to make gaze shifts toward the sound sources. Onset latency of the auriculomotor responses dropped to a remarkable 29 ms and the responses were resistant to extinction over the course of 125 trials.
evidence: This is cited from Siegmund and Santibáñez, 1982.

claim: Trained cats' pinna responses were resistant to extinction over the course of 125 trials.
source: The animals were then trained to make gaze shifts toward the sound sources. Onset latency of the auriculomotor responses dropped to a remarkable 29 ms and the responses were resistant to extinction over the course of 125 trials.
evidence: This is cited from Siegmund and Santibáñez, 1982.

claim: Populin and Yin (1998) replicated the findings of rapid pinna responses in trained cats with a mean onset latency of 26 ms.
source: Both findings were replicated by Populin and Yin, 1998 (mean = 26 ms; failure to extinguish across 10,000 unreinforced trials).
evidence: This is cited from Populin and Yin, 1998.

claim: Trained cats' pinna responses failed to extinguish across 10,000 unreinforced trials.
source: Both findings were replicated by Populin and Yin, 1998 (mean = 26 ms; failure to extinguish across 10,000 unreinforced trials).
evidence: This is cited from Populin and Yin, 1998.

claim: Populin and Yin obtained an even more rapid pinna response (mean = 21 ms) when the sound was preceded by a visual stimulus that served as warning signal and indicated that the cat should maintain gaze at a fixation point.
source: The latter authors obtained an even more rapid response (mean = 21 ms) when the sound was preceded by a visual stimulus that served as warning signal and indicated that the cat should maintain gaze at a fixation point.
evidence: This is cited from Populin and Yin, 1998.

claim: Populin and Yin argued that the short-latency pinna response is too rapid to be mediated by the superior colliculus.
source: They argued that the short-latency pinna response is too rapid to be mediated by the brain region most centrally involved in orienting, the superior colliculus (SC).
evidence: This is cited from Populin and Yin, 1998.

claim: The average first-spike latency in the relevant portion of the superior colliculus in cats is 19 ms.
source: This is because an earlier study, Populin and Yin, 1997, had found the average first-spike latency in the relevant portion of this structure to be 19 ms.
evidence: This is cited from Populin and Yin, 1997.

claim: Participants' auriculomotor responses may have been primarily of the short-latency variety that is not mediated by the superior colliculus.
source: Comparisons with these cat studies suggest that our participants' auriculomotor responses may have been primarily also of the short-latency variety that is not mediated by the SC.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with cat studies and the observed onset latencies.

claim: In cats, laterally presented task-relevant sounds during a delayed-saccade condition elicited ipsilateral pinna movements of the short-latency variety (21 ms).
source: During the delayed-saccade condition of their study, laterally presented sounds were task-relevant and forward fixation was required, as in our Experiment 2. Ipsilateral pinna movements triggered by onset of these sounds were of the short-latency variety (21 ms, as noted above).
evidence: This is cited from Populin and Yin, 1998.

claim: In cats, smaller pinna movements were observed in synchrony with ocular orienting, roughly 400 ms after the fixation point was extinguished.
source: Subsequent, smaller movements were then observed in synchrony with ocular orienting, roughly 400 ms after the fixation point was extinguished (Figure 7).
evidence: This is cited from Populin and Yin, 1998.

claim: Populin and Yin suggested that long-latency pinna movements might be mediated by the superior colliculus.
source: It is long-latency pinna movements of this sort that Populin and Yin, 1998 suggested might be mediated by the SC.
evidence: This is cited from Populin and Yin, 1998.

claim: The superior colliculus plays a major role in controlling eye fixation.
source: Given the major role of the SC in controlling eye fixation (Krauzlis et al., 2017), this structure may also be responsible for sustained maintenance of pinna orientation, such as in Experiment 2.
evidence: This is cited from Krauzlis et al., 2017.

claim: The superior colliculus may be responsible for sustained maintenance of pinna orientation.
source: Given the major role of the SC in controlling eye fixation (Krauzlis et al., 2017), this structure may also be responsible for sustained maintenance of pinna orientation, such as in Experiment 2.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of SC in eye fixation and the sustained nature of responses in Experiment 2.

claim: Pinna movements can be triggered by electrical stimulation of the deep and intermediate layers of the superior colliculus in accordance with a topographical pattern that is in register with that of eye movements.
source: Pinna movements can be triggered by electrical stimulation of the deep and intermediate layers of the SC in accordance with a topographical pattern that is in register with that of eye movements (Stein and Clamann, 1981).
evidence: This is cited from Stein and Clamann, 1981.

claim: Lesions of the superior colliculus reduce the likelihood of pinna orienting as well as its accuracy.
source: Lesions of this structure reduce the likelihood of pinna orienting as well as its accuracy, see Czihak et al., 1983.
evidence: This is cited from Czihak et al., 1983.

claim: Monosynaptic connections from the superior colliculus to auriculomotor neurons in the facial nucleus exist.
source: Although monosynaptic connections from SC to auriculomotor neurons in the facial nucleus do exist (Vidal et al., 1988), pinna control is dominated by disynaptic pathways from the SC that include the paralemniscal, oculomotor, or pontine reticular zones, see Henkel and Edwards, 1978; Takeuchi et al., 1979; Vidal et al., 1988.
evidence: This is cited from Vidal et al., 1988.

claim: Pinna control is dominated by disynaptic pathways from the superior colliculus that include the paralemniscal, oculomotor, or pontine reticular zones.
source: Although monosynaptic connections from SC to auriculomotor neurons in the facial nucleus do exist (Vidal et al., 1988), pinna control is dominated by disynaptic pathways from the SC that include the paralemniscal, oculomotor, or pontine reticular zones, see Henkel and Edwards, 1978; Takeuchi et al., 1979; Vidal et al., 1988.
evidence: This is cited from Henkel and Edwards, 1978; Takeuchi et al., 1979; Vidal et al., 1988.

claim: The paralemniscal zone appears to be the most important pathway for pinna control.
source: Among these, the paralemniscal zone appears to be the most important, and its auditory input originates in the nearby nucleus sagulum, see Henkel, 1981.
evidence: This is cited from Henkel, 1981.

claim: The auditory input to the paralemniscal zone originates in the nearby nucleus sagulum.
source: Among these, the paralemniscal zone appears to be the most important, and its auditory input originates in the nearby nucleus sagulum, see Henkel, 1981.
evidence: This is cited from Henkel, 1981.

claim: Lesions of auditory cortex reduce the kinematic complexity of pinna orienting and slow its habituation.
source: Lesions of auditory cortex reduce the kinematic complexity of pinna orienting and slow its habituation, see Alvarado and Santibañez, 1971.
evidence: This is cited from Alvarado and Santibañez, 1971.

claim: Stimulation and recording studies in the macaque have identified a premotor ear-eye field (area 8B), which is connected with both auditory cortical areas and the superior colliculus.
source: Stimulation and recording studies in the macaque have identified a premotor ear-eye field (area 8B), which is connected with both auditory cortical areas and the SC, see Lanzilotto et al., 2013.
evidence: This is cited from Lanzilotto et al., 2013.

claim: The eyes and pinnae work together during endogenously cued attentional orienting.
source: These animal neuroanatomy and physiology studies, coupled with Wilson, 1908 seminal report, make it clear that the eyes and pinnae work together during endogenously cued attentional orienting.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited animal studies and Wilson's report.

claim: A recent study in humans showed a close relationship between movements of the left and right eardrums and multiple parameters of task-related left- and right-directed eye movements.
source: A recent study in humans by Gruters et al., 2018, showed a close relationship between movements of the left and right eardrums and multiple parameters of task-related left- and right-directed eye movements.
evidence: This is cited from Gruters et al., 2018.

claim: Patterns of auricular muscle activity might serve as an easily accessible correlate of top-down processing in endogenous modes of attention.
source: They suggest that patterns of auricular muscle activity might serve as an easily accessible correlate of top-down processing in endogenous modes of attention.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings of the study.

claim: Auricular muscle activity effects might complement electroencephalographic indices of attentional focus.
source: As such, the described effects might complement electroencephalographic indices of attentional focus (de Cheveigné et al., 2018; Schäfer et al., 2018) in that their sensitivity is exclusively spatial, rather than reflecting a context-specific mixture of modality, feature, location, and object representations.
evidence: This is speculated based on comparison with EEG-based methods.

claim: Auricular muscle activity sensitivity is exclusively spatial, rather than reflecting a context-specific mixture of modality, feature, location, and object representations.
source: As such, the described effects might complement electroencephalographic indices of attentional focus (de Cheveigné et al., 2018; Schäfer et al., 2018) in that their sensitivity is exclusively spatial, rather than reflecting a context-specific mixture of modality, feature, location, and object representations.
evidence: This is inferred from the nature of the auricular responses observed.

claim: Registration of pinna-orienting might better support near real-time decoding of the attentional focus compared to EEG-based stimulus reconstruction approaches.
source: Registration of pinna-orienting might better support near real-time decoding of the attentional focus and, as compared to EEG-based stimulus reconstruction approaches, does not require the exogenous sound source, for example see the discussion in Schäfer et al., 2018.
evidence: This is speculated based on the properties of the auricular responses.

claim: Auricular muscle monitoring might support the decoding of auditory attention in technical applications such as attentionally controlled hearing aids.
source: Thus, auricular muscle monitoring might support the decoding of auditory attention in technical applications such as attentionally controlled hearing aids that preferentially amplify sounds the user is attempting to listen to.
evidence: This is speculated as a potential application of the findings.

claim: Both older (N = 12, mean age = 62.7 ± 5.9 y, 8 F, all right-handed) and younger adult (N = 16, mean age = 24.1 ± 3.1 y, 8 F, 15 right-handed, one left-handed) volunteers in Experiment one had age-typical, pure tone audiometric thresholds.
source: Both older (N = 12, mean age = 62.7 ± 5.9 y, 8 F, all right-handed) and younger adult (N = 16, mean age = 24.1 ± 3.1 y, 8 F, 15 right-handed, one left-handed) volunteers in Experiment one had age-typical, pure tone audiometric thresholds (1, 2, 4, and 8 kHz; young < 20 dB; old < 40 dB).
evidence: This describes the participant characteristics in the study.

claim: Only data from the final 21 subjects were retained for Experiment 2.
source: All served in both studies, but after the 8th participant, Experiment two was altered in several ways (e.g., four stimulus directions rather than two). Only data from the final 21 subjects were retained for Experiment 2.
evidence: This describes the methodological decision in the study.

claim: The study was approved by the ethics commission at the Ärztekammer des Saarlandes, Saarbrücken, Germany (Identification Number: 79/16).
source: The study was approved by the responsible ethics committee (ethics commission at the Ärztekammer des Saarlandes, Saarbrücken, Germany; Identification Number: 79/16).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: In Experiment 1, sounds lasted 1.7 – 10.0 s, were delivered every 15 – 40 s, and had an average intensity of 70 dBC, except for foot steps (65 dBC).
source: In Experiment 1, sounds lasted 1.7 – 10.0 s, were delivered every 15 – 40 s, and had an average intensity of 70 dBC, except for foot steps (65 dBC).
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters in Experiment 1.

claim: Each of the nine stimuli in Experiment 1 was repeated four times (once per speaker).
source: Each of the nine stimuli (lemur howling, dog barking, helicopter flying, cell phone vibrating, birds singing, baby crying, mosquito buzzing, footsteps, and traffic jam) was repeated four times (i.e., once per speaker).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, the stories were 5 min long, with an average intensity of 50 dBA for younger and 60 dBA for older participants.
source: In Experiment 2, the stories were 5 min long, with an average intensity of 50 dBA for younger and 60 dBA for older participants.
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters in Experiment 2.

claim: Surface EMGs were recorded with non-recessed, Ag/AgCl electrodes which were 4 mm in diameter for TAM and 6 mm in all other cases.
source: Surface EMGs were recorded with non-recessed, Ag/AgCl electrodes (BME4, BioMed Electrodes, USA), which were 4 mm in diameter for TAM and 6 mm (BME6) in all other cases, see Figure 1.
evidence: This describes the recording methodology.

claim: The signals were AD-converted at 9600 Hz and 24 bit resolution per channel.
source: The signals were AD-converted at 9600 Hz and 24 bit resolution per channel (4 × USBamp, g.tec GmbH, Austria).
evidence: This describes the data acquisition parameters.

claim: Preliminary tests with a participant who exhibited a large, reliable Wilson's phenomenon and who could voluntarily contract her SAM and PAM indicated that EMG from TAM electrodes was not an artifact of volume conduction from PAM or SAM.
source: Because surface electrodes had not previously been used to record from intrinsic ear muscles, we conducted preliminary tests with a participant who exhibited a large, reliable Wilson's phenomenon and who could voluntarily contract her SAM and PAM. Isolation of the corresponding responses indicated that EMG from TAM electrodes was not an artifact of volume conduction from PAM or SAM.
evidence: This describes validation of the recording methodology.

claim: The TAM activity was not correlated with forced SAM/PAM innervation.
source: In other words, the TAM activity was not correlated with forced SAM/PAM innervation.
evidence: This describes validation of the recording methodology.
